display.text: Unitless measure from −1 to 1 of the direction and strength of a linear relationship. Its magnitude near 1 indicates a strong linear association; near 0 indicates little linear association, not necessarily no relationship. This measure is Pearson's correlation, denoted r.
Prediction at an explanatory-variable value outside the range used to fit the model; the observed relationship may not continue there.
Predicted response at X = 0 in the line Ŷ = a + bX; calculated as a = Ȳ − bX̄ and potentially outside the meaningful data range.
Rule selecting a fitted line by minimizing the sum of squared vertical deviations from it.
Line that minimizes the sum of squared vertical deviations between observed responses and the line's predictions.
Linear association in which larger values of one variable tend to accompany smaller values of the other; r < 0.
Linear association in which larger values of one variable tend to accompany larger values of the other; r > 0.
Response obtained by substituting a specified explanatory-variable value into the fitted regression equation.
Method for specifying how a response variable depends on an explanatory variable and using that relationship for prediction.
Under the null of zero population slope, the probability of a test statistic at least as extreme as observed; measures evidence of a linear relationship, whereas r measures its sample strength.
Regression describing a quantitative response with a straight-line function of one explanatory variable.
Change in the fitted mean response for a one-unit increase in X. For simple least-squares regression, b = r(SY/SX).
Test of a population linear relationship, with null hypothesis that the population slope is zero; the usual two-sided alternative is a nonzero slope.
